note: Navarre and Aragon were united under Sancho III 'the Great' of Pamplona (1004–1035), who also controlled Castile and León temporarily — the closest medieval Iberia came to a single Christian kingdom before Ferdinand and Isabella. His death produced the familiar disaster: partition among sons. Aragon (under Ramiro I) and Navarre (under García III) became separate kingdoms that only reunited briefly under Alfonso I 'the Battler' (ruled both 1104–1134). Alfonso I's death without heirs permanently separated them: Aragon passed to Ramon Berenguer IV through marriage; Navarre elected García Ramírez.

_quarry.structural_significance: The Sancho III unification is the high point of early Navarrese-Aragonese power; the subsequent partition models the repeated failure of Iberian unification through personal union; the permanent Aragon-Navarre split after 1134 determines the subsequent structure of Iberian kingdoms — Aragon becomes a Mediterranean empire while Navarre becomes a French borderland
